summary: Describes RC2, a secret-key block encryption algorithm, that was offered as a possible replacement for DES. It is informational and documents the algorithm rather than endorsing it.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2268 is the written recipe for RC2, a secret-key cipher that scrambles data in 64-bit blocks. It was designed to be fast on small computers and to accept keys of any length from 1 to 128 bytes.

subtitle: A variable-key-size, 64-bit block cipher designed to run quickly on 16-bit microprocessors.

tldr.problem: A secret-key block cipher was wanted that could be proposed as a DES replacement and that would be easy to implement on 16-bit microprocessors.
tldr.mechanism: RC2 expands a key of 1 to 128 bytes into 64 words of 16 bits, then runs a 64-bit block through 16 mixing rounds and 2 mashing rounds that use those words.
tldr.outcome: The memo documents the algorithm with test vectors and gives an object identifier for RC2 in cipher block chaining mode. It is Informational, and it does not endorse RC2 as a standard.

facts.label: Key size
facts.value: 1 to 128 bytes, eight in the current implementation

today: RFC 2268 is an Informational memo from March 1998, and the metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It documents the RC2 algorithm and its object identifier rather than defining a standard, and it carries a notice that RC2 is a registered trademark of RSA Data Security, Inc.

sections.title: What RC2 Is
sections.content:
This memo, an RSA Laboratories Technical Note, describes RC2, a conventional secret-key block encryption algorithm that may be considered a proposal for a DES replacement. The input and output block sizes are 64 bits each. The key size is variable, from one byte up to 128 bytes, although the current implementation uses eight bytes.

The algorithm is designed to be easy to implement on 16-bit microprocessors. On an IBM AT, the encryption runs about twice as fast as DES, assuming that key expansion has been done.

Three separate algorithms are involved. Key expansion takes a variable-length input key and produces an expanded key consisting of 64 words, K[0] to K[63]. Encryption takes a 64-bit input quantity stored in words R[0] to R[3] and encrypts it in place, leaving the result in those words. Decryption is the inverse operation.

The memo fixes its notation. A word is a 16-bit quantity, + is twos-complement addition, & is the bitwise and, XOR is the bitwise exclusive-or, ~ is bitwise complement, ^ is exponentiation and MOD is the modulo operation. The memo also carries an intellectual property notice: RC2 is a registered trademark of RSA Data Security, Inc., whose RC2 software is available under licence from RSA Data Security, Inc.
sections.plainLanguage: RC2 scrambles a message in fixed-size pieces using a secret key. It was built to be quick on small, old computers, and it is careful to spell out every step so that anyone can write the same thing.

sections.title: Key Expansion
sections.content:
Because the algorithm deals with both eight-bit byte operations and 16-bit word operations, the key buffer is given two names: K[0] to K[63] for word operations, where each K[i] is a 16-bit word, and L[0] to L[127] for byte operations, where each L[i] is an eight-bit byte. These are two views of the same buffer, and at all times K[i] = L[2*i] + 256*L[2*i+1], so the low-order byte of each word comes first.

Exactly T bytes of key are assumed to be supplied, for some T in the range 1 to 128, and the current implementation uses T = 8. Regardless of T, the algorithm has a maximum effective key length in bits, denoted T1, and the search space is 2^(8*T) or 2^T1, whichever is smaller. The purpose of key expansion is to modify the key buffer so that each bit of the expanded key depends in a complicated way on every bit of the supplied input key.

The supplied key is placed into bytes L[0] to L[T-1]. The effective key length in bytes T8 and a mask TM are then computed from T1 by T8 = (T1+7)/8 and TM = 255 MOD 2^(8 + T1 - 8*T8), so TM has its 8 - (8*T8 - T1) least significant bits set. With an effective key length of 64 bits, T1 = 64, T8 = 8 and TM = 0xff; with 63 bits, T1 = 63, T8 = 8 and TM = 0x7f.

The expansion itself is two loops and an intermediate step, using PITABLE, an array of random bytes based on the digits of PI, which is a random permutation of the values 0 to 255. The first loop, for i = T to 127, sets L[i] = PITABLE[L[i-1] + L[i-T], with that addition modulo 256. The intermediate step sets L[128-T8] = PITABLE[L[128-T8] & TM], which reduces the search space so that the effective number of key bits is T1. The second loop, for i = 127-T8 down to 0, sets L[i] = PITABLE[L[i+1] XOR L[i+T8]]. The effective key consists of the values L[128-T8] to L[127], and the expanded key depends only on those effective key bits regardless of the supplied key K. Because the expanded key is not modified during encryption or decryption, the memo notes that one can expand the key just once when encrypting or decrypting a large block of data.
sections.plainLanguage: Before scrambling anything, RC2 stretches the secret key into a list of 64 numbers by mixing it with a fixed table derived from the digits of pi. Every bit of the result depends on the whole key, so a small change to the key changes everything.

sections.title: Encryption
sections.content:
Encryption is defined in terms of two primitive operations, mix and mash, and the expression x rol k denotes the 16-bit word x rotated left by k bits, with the bits shifted out of the top end entering the bottom end.

The mix operation on R[i] adds the next unused key word K[j] and a composite word built from the neighbouring words, then rotates the result left by s[i] bits, where s[0] is 1, s[1] is 2, s[2] is 3 and s[3] is 5. The indices of R are always considered modulo 4, so R[i-1] refers to R[3] when i is 0. The composite word is identical to R[i-2] in the positions where R[i-1] is one, and identical to R[i-3] in the positions where R[i-1] is zero. The variable j is global, so K[j] is always the first key word in the expanded key not yet used in a mix operation, and it is advanced after each use.

The mash operation adds to R[i] the key word K[R[i-1] & 63], that is, the key word chosen by the low-order six bits of R[i-1]. A mixing round mixes R[0], R[1], R[2] and R[3] in that order; a mashing round mashes the same four words in the same order.

The whole encryption operation starts by putting the 64-bit input value into R[0] to R[3], expanding the key, and setting j to zero. It then performs five mixing rounds, one mashing round, six mixing rounds, one mashing round and five mixing rounds. The memo notes that each mixing round uses four key words and there are 16 mixing rounds altogether, so each key word is used exactly once in a mixing round, while the mashing rounds refer to up to eight of the key words in a data-dependent manner, with repetitions possible and the set of words varying from encryption to encryption.
sections.plainLanguage: The block is held as four 16-bit numbers. Each round adds a number from the key list to each of them, mixes in what the neighbouring numbers hold, and shifts the bits around.

sections.title: Decryption
sections.content:
Decryption is defined in terms of primitives that undo the mix and mash operations, named r-mix and r-mash, where the r- denotes the reverse operation. The expression x ror k denotes the 16-bit word x rotated right by k bits, with the bits shifted out of the bottom end entering the top end.

The r-mix operation rotates R[i] right by s[i] bits, then subtracts K[j] and the same composite word built from the neighbours, and decrements j, so K[j] is always the key word with the greatest index not yet used in an r-mix. The r-mash operation subtracts from R[i] the key word K[R[i-1] & 63]. An r-mixing round processes R[3], R[2], R[1] and R[0] in that order, and an r-mashing round does the same.

The whole decryption operation mirrors encryption. It initialises R[0] to R[3] with the 64-bit ciphertext value, expands the key, sets j to 63, and then performs five r-mixing rounds, one r-mashing round, six r-mixing rounds, one r-mashing round and five r-mixing rounds.
sections.plainLanguage: Decryption runs the same steps backwards: rotate the other way, take the key numbers away instead of adding them, and work through the four words in the opposite order.

sections.title: Test Vectors and the CBC Object Identifier
sections.content:
The memo gives eight test vectors so that implementers can check their code, all in hexadecimal, with key lengths from 1 to 33 bytes and effective key lengths from 63 to 129 bits. The first has a key length of 8 bytes, an effective key length of 63 bits, a key of all zeros and a plaintext of all zeros, and gives the ciphertext ebb773f9 93278eff. The last has a key length of 33 bytes and an effective key length of 129 bits, and gives the ciphertext 5b78d3a4 3dfff1f1.

Section 6 gives the object identifier for RC2 in cipher block chaining mode: rc2CBC OBJECT IDENTIFIER ::= {iso(1) member-body(2) US(840) rsadsi(113549) encryptionAlgorithm(3) 2}. RC2-CBC takes parameters that are either a simple 8-octet initialisation vector or a sequence of a version number and an initialisation vector, where the initialisation vector is an octet string of 8 octets and the version is an integer in the range 1 to 1024.

The memo explains that RC2 in CBC mode has two parameters, an 8-byte initialisation vector and a version number in the range 1 to 1024, which specifies in a roundabout manner the number of effective key bits used for the RC2 encryption or decryption. If the number of effective key bits is in the range 1 to 255, the version number is given by a 256-byte translation table specified in the memo, which is a permutation on the numbers 0 to 255 and is not the same table used in the key expansion phase. If the number of effective key bits is in the range 256 to 1024, the version number is simply the number of effective key bits. The default number of effective key bits for RC2 is 32, and in that case the parameters should be supplied as a simple initialisation vector rather than as a sequence containing a version and an initialisation vector.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo includes worked examples so a programmer can check that their implementation gives the same answers, and it names the algorithm so that a protocol can refer to RC2 in CBC mode.

items.title: Key expansion
items.text: Turns a key of 1 to 128 bytes into 64 words of 16 bits.

items.title: Mix
items.text: Adds the next key word and a word built from the neighbours, then rotates.

items.title: Mash
items.text: Adds the key word chosen by the low six bits of the previous word.

items.title: Mixing round
items.text: Mixes R[0], R[1], R[2] and R[3] in that order.

items.title: Mashing round
items.text: Mashes the same four words in the same order.

items.title: The round schedule
items.text: 5 mixing rounds, 1 mashing round, 6 mixing rounds, 1 mashing round, 5 mixing rounds.

viz.caption: THE ENCRYPTION OPERATION AS THE MEMO LISTS IT

data.title: RC2 encryption steps
data.code:
1. Initialize words R[0], ..., R[3] to contain the 64-bit input value.
2. Expand the key, so that words K[0], ..., K[63] become defined.
3. Initialize j to zero.
4. Perform five mixing rounds.
5. Perform one mashing round.
6. Perform six mixing rounds.
7. Perform one mashing round.
8. Perform five mixing rounds.
